_README: Executables that appear in ONE builder's workflow and not the other.
run_pseudo_build_gate.py fails if this file and the observed difference
disagree in either direction, so adding a stage to either builder forces
an explicit decision here: port it, or write down why not.
'verified' says HOW the equivalence was established. 'artifact' means the
two generated scripts were read side by side and run the same programs on
the same inputs. 'role' means only the intent matches and the
implementations are independent -- those are the entries that can drift
silently, and the ones a reviewer should look at first.
Last verified 2026-08-22 against PR #181 head ba171c5.
WHAT THIS CHECK DOES NOT COVER, so nobody reads more into a green run:
* It compares executable BASENAMES of jobs in the TOP-LEVEL DAG. It does
not descend into SUBDAG EXTERNAL nodes, so a stage that lives only
inside a sub-workflow is invisible to it.
* A new stage added under an ALREADY-PRESENT basename does not change
the difference set and will not be reported.
* It says nothing about the CONTENTS of the generated .sh wrappers
(con_marg.sh, con_prod.sh, join_post.sh, terminal_collect_extrinsic.sh).
That is exactly where the 'role' equivalences below live, so those
entries can drift without this gate noticing.
In short: it catches a builder growing a new top-level stage, which is
the drift that has actually happened. It is not a proof of parity.
'shared-code' is stronger than 'artifact': the two sides are emitted by
one generator, so agreement is structural rather than observed once.
Moving an entry there is the way to retire it -- an 'artifact' entry only
records that two independent generators agreed on the day someone looked.

allinone_convert.sh.note: Both sides are now generated by RIFT.misc.extrinsic_stage, so the commands cannot drift; only the paths differ, and that difference is structural (per-iteration ILE directory vs terminal stage directory). Verified token-identical against the pre-extraction build. Guarded by test_extrinsic_stage_shared.py, which also fails if either builder starts deriving --n-eff or the distance-slice flags itself.

convert_output_format_ile2inference.note: BasicIteration runs this as its own DAG node; Hyperpipe calls the same executable from inside its generated collector, so it never appears as a submit executable. Same program, same --convention LI --export-cosmology --use-interpolated-cosmology arguments. This is coverage that is invisible to a node-level comparison -- the reason this ledger records the mechanism and not just the name.

consolidate_dgrid.sh.note: BasicIteration wraps the executable in a generated shell script; Hyperpipe invokes it directly as a command-v1 terminal stage. Same --input-glob/--output shape. The GLOBS DIFFER (iteration_*_ile/EXTR_out*.xml_*_.dgrid vs terminal_extrinsic/EXTR_out*.xml_*_.dgrid) because the two builders put the extrinsic output in different directories; that the resulting products agree is NOT established here -- see M7 in the paper-repo record.

consolidate_dslice.sh.note: As consolidate_dgrid.sh, with --dslice products. Same caveat: equal command shape is not equal output.

join_grids.sh.note: Both join the exploded posterior workers into the next iteration's grid. Implementations are INDEPENDENT: BasicIteration runs util_RandomizeOverlapOrder.py over overlap-grid-*.xml.gz; Hyperpipe's join_post.sh copies the ASCII header with awk and shuffles output-*.dat with shuf. Different code, different format, same intent -- the clearest drift candidate in this table.

util_ILEdagPostprocess.sh.note: BasicIteration consolidates one iteration's ILE output with the in-tree util_ILEdagPostprocess.sh. Hyperpipe splits the job in two: util_CleanILE_hyperpipeline.py per event, then util_HyperCombine.py --combination product across events. With a single ILE marg driver the product is over one input and should be the identity, but that is an ASSUMPTION, not a measurement: if a second marg driver is ever configured, the two builders stop meaning the same thing.
